Duke Ellington was an American jazz composer, bandleader, and pianist whose sophisticated orchestrations and extended compositions established him as one of the most important musicians in twentieth-century American music.

As bandleader of the Duke Ellington Orchestra, one of the longest continuously performing orchestras in history, he created a laboratory for complex harmonic arrangements. He composed thousands of works including suite-length pieces like "Black, Brown and Beige" from 1943, which explored African-American history through orchestral jazz.

He created signature arrangements that showcased individual band members' timbres. The Ellington Sound featured growling trumpets and muted brass effects. His iconic compositions include "Mood Indigo," "Take the A Train," "It Don't Mean a Thing If It Ain't Got That Swing," and "Satin Doll."

Ellington pioneered jazz education through concert tours at universities and demonstrated that jazz could achieve the artistic weight of classical symphonic music. He performed at Carnegie Hall in 1943 and represented American jazz internationally for over fifty years. He influenced the next generation of composers like Charles Mingus, who extended his orchestral ambitions, and established jazz's concert-music aspirations.
